title: Problem Statement and Imports
content: The docstring presents Erdős Problem #1093 on the deficiency of binomial coefficients: for $n \geq 2k$, the deficiency counts how many of $n, n-1, \ldots, n-k+1$ are $k$-smooth (all prime factors $\leq k$), under the condition that $\binom{n}{k}$ has no prime factor $\leq k$. Erdős, Lacampagne, and Selfridge (1988, 1993) asked (i) whether infinitely many pairs have deficiency 1, and (ii) whether only finitely many have deficiency $> 1$. Imports include `Nat.Prime.Basic`, `Nat.Choose.Basic`, `Nat.Factorization.Basic`, `Finset.Card`, and `Real.Sqrt`.
mathContext: The binomial coefficient $\binom{n}{k} = \frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!} = \frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)}{k!}$. The condition $\text{NoSmallPrimeFactors}(n,k)$ requires every prime $p \mid \binom{n}{k}$ to satisfy $p > k$. This is a strong sieve condition: the 'small' primes in the falling factorial $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ must cancel exactly with $k!$.

title: $k$-Smooth Numbers
content: Defines `IsKSmooth k m`: a positive integer $m$ is $k$-smooth if every prime factor of $m$ is $\leq k$. These are numbers composed entirely of 'small' primes. The concept originates in computational number theory where $B$-smooth numbers play a central role in factoring algorithms (quadratic sieve, number field sieve). In the context of deficiency, $k$-smooth terms in the falling factorial are the ones whose prime factors are 'absorbed' by $k!$.
mathContext: $\text{IsKSmooth}(k, m) \iff \forall p \text{ prime},\, p \mid m \implies p \leq k$. Equivalently, $m = \prod_{p \leq k} p^{a_p}$ for some exponents $a_p \geq 0$. The count of $k$-smooth numbers up to $x$ is $\Psi(x, k) \sim x \cdot u^{-u}$ where $u = \log x / \log k$ (Dickman's function), a fundamental result in analytic number theory.

title: No Small Prime Factors Condition
content: Defines `NoSmallPrimeFactors n k`: every prime dividing $\binom{n}{k}$ exceeds $k$. This means the product $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ has enough small prime factors to exactly cancel with $k!$. The condition is quite restrictive: it requires the falling factorial to have precisely the right smooth structure. Kummer's theorem (1852) characterizes primes dividing binomial coefficients via carries in base-$p$ addition, providing a tool for verifying this condition.
mathContext: $\text{NoSmallPrimeFactors}(n, k) \iff \forall p \leq k,\, p \text{ prime} \implies v_p(\binom{n}{k}) = 0$, where $v_p$ denotes the $p$-adic valuation. By Kummer's theorem, $v_p(\binom{n}{k})$ equals the number of carries when adding $k$ and $n-k$ in base $p$. So $\text{NoSmallPrimeFactors}$ requires zero carries for all primes $p \leq k$.

title: The Deficiency Function
content: Defines `deficiency n k` as the cardinality of $\{i \in [0, k) : n - i \text{ is } k\text{-smooth}\}$ using `Finset.filter`. The deficiency counts how many terms in the falling factorial $n, n-1, \ldots, n-k+1$ have all prime factors $\leq k$. A deficiency of 0 means none of the terms are smooth; deficiency 1 means exactly one is. The definition is noncomputable since `IsKSmooth` involves quantification over all primes.
mathContext: $\text{deficiency}(n, k) = |\{0 \leq i < k : \text{IsKSmooth}(k, n-i)\}|$. Under the $\text{NoSmallPrimeFactors}$ condition, the $k$-smooth terms are precisely those whose prime factors are 'used up' by $k!$ in the formula $\binom{n}{k} = \prod_{i=0}^{k-1}(n-i)/k!$. The deficiency measures the 'excess smoothness' in the falling factorial beyond what $k!$ requires.

title: Part (i): Infinitely Many Deficiency 1
content: The first conjecture: $\text{Set.Infinite}\{(k, n) : 2k \leq n \land \text{NoSmallPrimeFactors}(n, k) \land \text{deficiency}(n, k) = 1\}$. This asks whether there are infinitely many binomial coefficients with no small prime factors and exactly one $k$-smooth term in the falling factorial. At least 58 such examples are known for $n \leq 10^5$, including $\binom{7}{3} = 35$ and $\binom{13}{4} = 715$. The conjecture is supported by computational evidence but no theoretical progress exists.
mathContext: Examples: $\binom{7}{3} = 35 = 5 \times 7$ (no prime $\leq 3$ divides 35), falling factorial terms $7, 6, 5$: only $6 = 2 \times 3$ is 3-smooth, so deficiency = 1. $\binom{13}{4} = 715 = 5 \times 11 \times 13$ (no prime $\leq 4$ divides 715), terms $13, 12, 11, 10$: checking which are 4-smooth gives deficiency = 1.

title: Part (ii): Finitely Many Deficiency $> 1$
content: The second conjecture: $\text{Set.Finite}\{(k, n) : 2k \leq n \land \text{NoSmallPrimeFactors}(n, k) \land \text{deficiency}(n, k) > 1\}$. This is stronger than Part (i) and asserts that high deficiency is a genuinely rare phenomenon. The record is $\binom{284}{28}$ with deficiency 9. If true, there exists a uniform bound on the deficiency for all sufficiently large $n$ and $k$. The ELS upper bound $n \ll 2^k \sqrt{k}$ constrains the search region but does not directly resolve finiteness.
mathContext: If Part (ii) is true, then $\exists N,\, \forall (n, k)$ with $n \geq N$ and $2k \leq n$: $\text{NoSmallPrimeFactors}(n, k) \implies \text{deficiency}(n, k) \leq 1$. Combined with Part (i), this would mean deficiency 1 occurs infinitely often but deficiency $\geq 2$ is a finite (and presumably small) phenomenon.

title: Known Examples and Computed Values
content: Three axioms record specific deficiency computations. $\binom{7}{3} = 35$: among $\{7, 6, 5\}$, only $6 = 2 \times 3$ is 3-smooth, giving deficiency 1. $\binom{13}{4} = 715$: deficiency 1. $\binom{284}{28}$: deficiency 9, the highest known. The case $\binom{284}{28}$ is remarkable—among the 28 consecutive integers $284, 283, \ldots, 257$, exactly 9 are 28-smooth while $\binom{284}{28}$ has no prime factor $\leq 28$. This extreme concentration of smooth numbers in a short interval is the phenomenon the conjecture seeks to bound.
mathContext: For $\binom{284}{28}$, the 28-smooth numbers among $\{257, 258, \ldots, 284\}$ are those with all prime factors in $\{2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23\}$. Having 9 such numbers in an interval of length 28 is an unusually high density of smooth numbers—Dickman's function predicts roughly $28 \cdot \rho(\log 284 / \log 28) \approx 28 \cdot \rho(1.7) \approx 28 \times 0.45 \approx 13$ smooth numbers, so 9 with the additional NoSmallPrimeFactors constraint is not implausible.

title: ELS Upper Bound: $n \ll 2^k \sqrt{k}$
content: Erdős, Lacampagne, and Selfridge (1993) proved that if $(n, k)$ has positive deficiency and $n \geq 2k$, then $n \leq C \cdot 2^k \sqrt{k}$ for an absolute constant $C$. This exponential bound in $k$ means that for each fixed $k$, only finitely many $n$ can have positive deficiency—but the bound grows exponentially with $k$, so it does not immediately resolve Part (ii). The proof uses sieve methods and estimates on the distribution of smooth numbers.
mathContext: $\text{deficiency}(n, k) \geq 1 \implies n \leq C \cdot 2^k \cdot k^{1/2}$. Since the falling factorial has $k$ terms in $[n-k+1, n]$, and at least one must be $k$-smooth, this constrains how large $n$ can be: if $n \gg 2^k$, the terms $n - i$ are too large to be $k$-smooth (since $\Psi(x, k) / x \to 0$ as $x/k \to \infty$). The $\sqrt{k}$ factor comes from refined sieve estimates.

title: Computational Census: At Least 58 Examples
content: At least 58 pairs $(k, n)$ with deficiency 1 are known for $n \leq 10^5$. This computational result supports Part (i) of the conjecture. The formalization uses a product of finite ranges `Finset.range 100 ×ˢ Finset.range 100001` and filters for the deficiency-1 condition. The count of 58 provides evidence for infinitude but does not constitute a proof, since an arithmetic phenomenon can have many small examples and still be finite.
mathContext: $|\{(k, n) : k < 100, n < 100001, 2k \leq n, \text{deficiency}(n, k) = 1\}| \geq 58$. For comparison, the twin prime counting function $\pi_2(10^5) \approx 1224$, so deficiency-1 pairs are much rarer than twin primes in the same range.

title: Proved: Large Factor Exclusion
content: The one fully proved theorem: if $n - i$ has a prime factor $p > k$, then $n - i$ is not $k$-smooth, so it does not contribute to the deficiency. The proof is by direct contradiction: if $n - i$ were $k$-smooth, then every prime factor would be $\leq k$, contradicting $p > k$ and $p \mid (n-i)$. The Lean proof uses `omega` after unpacking the definitions. This is a structural lemma confirming that the definitions compose correctly.
mathContext: $p > k \land p \text{ prime} \land p \mid (n-i) \implies \neg\text{IsKSmooth}(k, n-i)$. Proof: $\text{IsKSmooth}(k, n-i)$ requires all prime factors $\leq k$, but $p \mid (n-i)$ and $p > k$, contradiction. This is trivial mathematically but serves as a sanity check that `IsKSmooth` and `deficiency` interact correctly in the formalization.
